note: For each combination of answers, the rule with the highest priority applies; with equal priority, the rule with the most matching conditions. The validator checks that there is always exactly one.

models.name: Mean and standard deviation, and median and interquartile range
models.description: Report both: mean (SD) and median [IQR], with a confidence interval for the main estimate. If the mean and the median differ noticeably, the distribution is probably skewed, and the median [IQR] is usually the more representative summary.
assumptions: Compare mean and median, and look at a histogram or box plot, to judge whether the distribution is symmetric
With repeated measurements, describe each measurement occasion separately.
The coefficients of a descriptive regression describe differences in the data; adjusting for other variables changes their meaning and does not make them causal
models.measure: Mean (SD) and median [IQR]; mean difference with 95% CI when describing groups

alternatives.name: Simple linear regression (descriptive)
alternatives.when: To describe how the mean of the outcome differs between groups or along a variable: each coefficient is the difference in means per category or per unit, read as a description, not as a causal effect

alternatives.name: Direct standardisation
alternatives.when: Comparing populations with a different structure (for example age): the summaries are computed as if the populations had the same structure

models.name: Frequencies and proportions with confidence intervals
models.description: Number and percentage for each category, with the denominator stated and a score (Wilson) confidence interval for proportions.
assumptions: Define the target population, the time and the measure (for example prevalence on a given date)
Simple (Wald) intervals can be inaccurate with small samples or proportions near 0 or 1

alternatives.name: Stratified proportions
alternatives.when: Describing the outcome in subgroups chosen in advance (for example by sex or age group)

alternatives.name: Directly standardised prevalence
alternatives.when: Comparing populations with a different structure, for example by age

models.measure: Proportion (prevalence or cumulative incidence) with 95% CI

models.name: Rates per person-time
models.description: Number of events divided by the total observation time, for example per 1000 person-years, with an exact (Poisson) confidence interval.
assumptions: The observation time of each subject needs to be known.

alternatives.name: Directly standardised rates
alternatives.when: Comparing populations with a different age structure; a gamma-based interval is suggested

alternatives.name: Standardised mortality (or incidence) ratio
alternatives.when: Comparing a population with reference rates (indirect standardisation)

models.measure: Rate per person-time with 95% CI

models.name: Kaplan-Meier curve
models.description: Survival curve with the number at risk below the plot, median survival and survival at fixed clinical time points.
assumptions: Censoring is non-informative: subjects who leave the study have the same risk as those who stay.
Late entry, loss to follow-up and competing events can bias the description

alternatives.name: Restricted mean survival time
alternatives.when: Summarising the average event-free time up to a fixed horizon

alternatives.name: Curves by stratum
alternatives.when: Describing subgroups chosen in advance

models.name: Cumulative incidence (Aalen-Johansen)
models.description: Cumulative incidence of each type of event. One minus Kaplan-Meier overestimates the risk when there are competing events.

models.name: Linear regression
models.description: Estimates the mean difference in the outcome between groups, or per unit of a covariate, adjusted for the other covariates.
models.simpleTest: Welch t-test for 2 groups; Mann-Whitney test if the distribution is very skewed and the sample is small; ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis for more than 2 groups.

alternatives.name: Ordinal regression (proportional odds model)
alternatives.when: Very skewed outcome or outliers

alternatives.name: Splines or fractional polynomials
alternatives.when: Non-linear relationship with a continuous covariate

models.measure: Mean difference (beta coefficient) with 95% CI
assumptions: Linear relationship with continuous covariates
Residuals with constant variance
Residuals roughly normal (less important in large samples)

models.name: Linear mixed model
models.description: Linear regression with random effects for the subject or the cluster. It uses all available measurements, even when some subjects have fewer.
models.simpleTest: Paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test for 2 paired measurements; repeated-measures ANOVA only if no data are missing.

alternatives.name: GEE
alternatives.when: The question is about the population-average effect, not the effect on the individual subject

models.measure: Mean difference with 95% CI
assumptions: Data missing at random (missingness explained by observed variables)
Appropriate correlation structure

models.name: Logistic regression
models.description: Estimates the adjusted odds ratio. For effects on common outcomes, the risk ratio estimated with modified Poisson regression can be added.
models.simpleTest: Chi-squared test; Fisher's exact test if any expected count is below 5.

alternatives.name: Modified Poisson (robust standard errors) or log-binomial regression
alternatives.when: Common outcome and the risk ratio is wanted

alternatives.name: Logistic regression with Firth's correction
alternatives.when: Few events or separation

models.measure: Odds ratio with 95% CI; risk ratio and absolute risks for clinicians
assumptions: Linearity on the logit scale for continuous covariates
Enough events per parameter

models.name: Mixed-effects logistic regression or GEE
models.description: The mixed model estimates an odds ratio conditional on the subject or cluster; GEE estimates a population-average odds ratio.

alternatives.name: GEE
alternatives.when: The question is about the population-average effect

models.measure: Odds ratio with 95% CI
assumptions: Enough clusters to estimate the between-cluster variance

models.name: Ordinal logistic regression (proportional odds)
models.description: Uses the whole order of the categories, without dichotomising the outcome.
models.simpleTest: Mann-Whitney test for 2 groups; Kruskal-Wallis test for more groups.

alternatives.name: Multinomial logistic regression
alternatives.when: The proportional odds assumption is clearly violated

models.measure: Common odds ratio across all cut-points, with 95% CI
assumptions: Proportional odds: the effect is the same at every cut-point of the outcome

models.name: Mixed-effects ordinal model
models.description: Proportional odds model with random effects for the subject or the cluster.
models.simpleTest: Wilcoxon signed-rank test for 2 paired measurements.
models.measure: Common odds ratio with 95% CI
assumptions: Proportional odds

models.name: Multinomial logistic regression
models.description: A set of odds ratios for each category against a reference category.
models.measure: Odds ratio per category with 95% CI
assumptions: Many parameters: many events are needed in each category

models.name: Mixed-effects multinomial model
models.description: Multinomial logistic regression with random effects for the subject or the cluster.
models.measure: Odds ratio per category with 95% CI
assumptions: Many parameters: many events are needed in each category

models.name: Poisson regression with an offset
models.description: Estimates the rate ratio. The offset (log of the observation time) accounts for subjects followed for different lengths of time.

alternatives.name: Negative binomial regression
alternatives.when: The variance is much larger than the mean (overdispersion)

alternatives.name: Zero-inflated models
alternatives.when: Many more zeros than the model predicts

models.measure: Rate ratio with 95% CI
assumptions: Variance equal to the mean (Poisson)
Independent events within the same subject

models.name: Mixed-effects Poisson or negative binomial model
models.description: Count model with random effects for the subject or the cluster.

alternatives.name: GEE for counts
alternatives.when: The question is about the population-average effect

models.measure: Rate ratio with 95% CI
assumptions: Check for overdispersion

models.name: Cox model
models.description: Estimates the adjusted hazard ratio. It is usually shown together with Kaplan-Meier curves.

alternatives.name: Restricted mean survival time (RMST)
alternatives.when: The hazard ratio changes over time, or a more intuitive measure is needed

alternatives.name: Flexible parametric models
alternatives.when: Absolute risk over time is needed, or extrapolation

models.measure: Hazard ratio with 95% CI; for clinicians, absolute risk at a fixed time and RMST
assumptions: Non-informative censoring
Proportional hazards: if they do not hold, hazard ratios by period or the RMST are options

models.name: Cox model with frailty or robust standard errors
models.description: Cox model with a random effect (frailty) for the cluster, or with robust standard errors for clustered subjects.
models.simpleTest: Kaplan-Meier curves and stratified log-rank test.
models.measure: Hazard ratio with 95% CI
assumptions: Proportional hazards
Non-informative censoring

models.name: Cause-specific Cox model
models.description: For an aetiological question: one Cox model for each type of event, treating competing events as censored. Reporting the cumulative incidence as well is recommended.

alternatives.name: Fine-Gray model
alternatives.when: Add it to describe the effect on the absolute risk

models.measure: Cause-specific hazard ratio with 95% CI, for each type of event
assumptions: Proportional hazards for each cause

models.name: Fine-Gray model
models.description: To predict the absolute risk of an event in the presence of competing events. Reporting the cause-specific hazards as well is recommended.
models.measure: Subdistribution hazard ratio and predicted cumulative incidence
assumptions: The subdistribution hazard ratio has no simple causal interpretation

models.name: Bland-Altman plot and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)
models.description: Bland-Altman for agreement between two methods (mean difference and limits of agreement); ICC for reliability between raters or repetitions.
models.measure: Mean difference and 95% limits of agreement; ICC with 95% CI
assumptions: Pearson's correlation is not a measure of agreement
It is recommended to state the type of ICC (model, type, definition)

models.name: Cohen's kappa (weighted for ordered categories)
models.description: Agreement between two raters beyond the agreement expected by chance. For ordered categories use weighted kappa.
models.measure: Kappa with 95% CI and raw percentage agreement
assumptions: Kappa depends on the prevalence of the categories: reporting raw agreement as well is recommended

models.name: Sensitivity, specificity and ROC curve
models.description: Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and likelihood ratios against the reference standard; ROC curve and AUC for continuous tests.
models.measure: Sensitivity and specificity with 95% CI; AUC with 95% CI
assumptions: Predictive values depend on the prevalence in the sample
The reference standard should be applied to all subjects

models.name: Logistic regression adjusted for the matching factors, or conditional logistic regression
models.description: Matching does not remove confounding by the matching factors: they need to be controlled in the analysis. With frequency matching or a few large strata, an ordinary (unconditional) logistic regression that includes the matching factors is usually adequate; with individual matching and many small strata, conditional logistic regression avoids sparse-data bias.
models.measure: Odds ratio with 95% CI
assumptions: The matching factors are included in the analysis
Matching on variables affected by the exposure or the outcome is generally discouraged

models.name: Linear mixed model with treatment and period effects
models.description: Within-subject comparison: treatment and period are fixed effects and the participant is a random effect. With two treatments and two periods, this is equivalent to comparing the within-subject period differences between the two sequence groups.
models.simpleTest: t-test (or Mann-Whitney test) on the period differences between the two sequence groups.
models.measure: Mean difference between treatments with 95% CI
assumptions: Carry-over effects should be ruled out, mainly with an adequate wash-out period
The analysis by sequence group separates period effects from treatment effects

models.name: Mixed-effects model for the type of outcome, with treatment and period effects
models.description: The same structure as for continuous outcomes, with the model suited to the outcome: mixed-effects logistic regression for binary outcomes, ordinal or multinomial models for categories, Poisson or negative binomial models for counts.
models.measure: Odds ratio or rate ratio between treatments with 95% CI
assumptions: Carry-over effects should be ruled out, mainly with an adequate wash-out period
Time-to-event outcomes rarely suit a cross-over design

models.name: g-methods: marginal structural model with inverse probability weights, g-formula or g-estimation
models.description: When confounders change over time and are affected by earlier exposure, standard regression adjustment is biased whether or not those confounders are included. g-methods estimate the effect of exposure strategies under weaker conditions.

alternatives.name: Target trial emulation with cloning, censoring and weighting
alternatives.when: Comparing sustained treatment strategies with observational data

models.measure: Contrast of outcomes under exposure strategies (risk difference, risk ratio or hazard ratio) with 95% CI, often by bootstrap
assumptions: Exchangeability, positivity and consistency at each time point
Check the distribution of the weights; truncation is an option when they are extreme
The models for exposure (weights) or for outcome and confounders (g-formula) need to be specified correctly

models.name: Random-effects meta-analysis (Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman)
models.description: Pools the effect estimates of the studies, allowing for real differences between them. The Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method gives more appropriate confidence intervals than the classic DerSimonian-Laird method.

alternatives.name: Common-effect (fixed-effect) meta-analysis
alternatives.when: The studies are assumed to estimate the same effect: it answers a narrower question

models.measure: Pooled effect on the scale of the studies (OR, RR, HR, mean difference) with 95% CI and 95% prediction interval
assumptions: Report heterogeneity: tau² and I²
Report the prediction interval: the range of effects expected in a new setting
Combine effect estimates on the same scale

models.name: Prevalent new-user design with time-conditional propensity scores
models.description: When many users of the newer drug switched from the comparator, an incident new-user design would exclude most of them. The prevalent new-user design defines exposure sets (by time or by number of prescriptions), computes time-conditional propensity scores of starting the newer drug, and matches each user of the newer drug to a comparator user with a similar score at the same point of treatment history. The outcome is then compared in the matched cohort, typically with a Cox model.

alternatives.name: Incident new-user, active-comparator design
alternatives.when: Enough patients start either drug for the first time

models.measure: Hazard ratio (or another measure suited to the outcome) with 95% CI in the matched cohort
assumptions: Time zero is aligned: follow-up starts at the switch for the newer drug and at the matched point for the comparator
Covariates are measured before time zero, not afterwards
Covariate balance is checked after matching
